title: Ashvatthama is dead
hookLine: Bhima kills an elephant, and then he shouts its name across the field
carry: satyam vada: even a half-truth costs

cards: There's an elephant on the Kaurava side named Ashvatthama. Same name as Drona's beloved son.
Bhima finds the elephant, kills it with his mace, and then turns toward Drona and shouts, loud enough for the whole field: Ashvatthama is dead. It's a trick, and it was planned.

Drona has been cutting through the Pandava army, and Krishna has told them, in Ganguli's telling, that the teacher can't be beaten while he holds his weapons. But if he hears that his son is dead, he'll put them down.
Today, how a truthful man's half-truth ends his teacher's life.

teach.b: Drona hears Bhima, and he doesn't believe it. Not from Bhima. There's one man whose word he trusts: Yudhishthira, known for never telling a lie.
So Drona asks him directly. Is my son dead? Arjuna won't have any part of the plan.
Krishna presses Yudhishthira: there are times, he argues, when a falsehood saves lives. Yudhishthira is afraid of lying, the text says, and he wants victory. So he answers: Ashvatthama is dead.
And under his breath, so Drona can't hear, he adds: the elephant. Then the epic adds a detail. Yudhishthira's chariot, the text says, had always moved a little above the earth.
After those words, it sinks and runs along the ground like everyone else's.
Drona, his heart broken, lays down his weapons. He sits on his chariot and turns inward, in yoga. Dhrishtadyumna, the prince of Panchala, rushes at him with a sword.
Arjuna cries out to take him alive. Too late. Dhrishtadyumna strikes, and the teacher of both houses is dead.
Here's what the epic won't let go of. The trick worked, and the war turned. But the man known for his truth paid with the thing he was known for, and the ground itself took note.
The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students a rule as they leave their teacher's house: satyam vada, speak the truth; dharmam chara, live by dharma. Yudhishthira's words were technically true.
Many teachers read the sinking chariot simply: a half-truth told to deceive weighs like a lie. Karna will lead next.

how: Yudhishthira's half-truth about Ashvatthama is told in the Drona Parva, and Hindu storytellers and teachers return to it when they talk about truthfulness, dharma and the costs of the war.

o: the teacher's son, whose name the slain elephant shares
the prince of Panchala who rushes in with a drawn sword
the teacher of both houses, who lays down his weapons in grief

p: said the elephant under his breath
refused the plan, cried take him alive

s: an elephant with the same name was killed; his son was alive.
Yudhishthira's chariot sank to the ground after his words
the text says it had moved above the earth until then.
Yudhishthira's half-truth didn't count against him, since his words were technically true
his chariot, which had moved above the earth, sank to the ground. satyam vada asks for the truth, not true-sounding words.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. your teacher asks you, the man who never lies, whether his son is dead. what do you say?
o: tell him plainly that his son is alive.
say Ashvatthama is dead, and whisper the elephant.
games.why: Yudhishthira says Ashvatthama is dead and adds the elephant under his breath. His chariot sinks to the ground.

practice: Satyam vada: speak the truth. Think of a time you told a half-truth, the true words with the important part said quietly or not at all, and go gently: no need to punish yourself.
Breathe in and remember what you said; breathe out and feel how it sat with you afterward, light or heavy. If you pray, you can bring that moment there; if not, just let it be seen.

wordCard.voice: Drona. The teacher of both houses, who laid down his weapons when the one man he trusted said his son was dead.
